title: Wall Street's AI Selloff Deepens as S&P 500 and Dow Confirm Correction
excerpt: The Nasdaq fell 5.28% on Friday and erased its 2026 gains as Anthropic's debut fizzled and Nvidia slid 13.8%, pushing the S&P 500 and the Dow more than 10% below their record closes.
body:
• Wall Street ended sharply lower on Friday as an AI selloff deepened: the Nasdaq Composite fell 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73, erasing its gains for 2026.
  • The S&P 500 lost 3.70% to 6,910.42 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.93% to 48,147.33 — both indexes are now more than 10% below their record closing highs, confirming a correction.
  • Anthropic's stock fell 9.1% on its second day of trading and Nvidia dropped 13.8%, as investors questioned how much of the AI story is already priced in with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%.
  • Markets are pricing a near-certain likelihood of a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool; the next test is next week's PCE inflation figures.

US stocks extended their rout on Friday, and the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic's momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year's stock market rally, Reuters reported. All three major indexes ended sharply lower, and the S&P 500 notched its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. The S&P 500 lost 265.41 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.42, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73. With Friday's close, the S&P 500 and the Dow are both more than 10% below their record closing highs — the technical definition of a correction — while the tech-heavy Nasdaq dipped into negative territory for the year. For the week, the Nasdaq fell about 10%, its biggest weekly decline since 2020, and the S&P 500 and the Dow logged their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when President Donald Trump's "liberation day" tariff package rattled markets.

What drove the selloff

The selling centered on the AI trade. Anthropic, which closed 17.1% above its $83 offer price on Thursday in a blockbuster debut, fell 9.1% on Friday, its second day as a public company. Nvidia tumbled 13.8% on Friday and 23% for the week after Reuters reported the Securities and Exchange Commission was probing its accounting, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 11% in a broad retreat from risk. The chip index had been up as much as 106.6% in mid-June; its year-to-date advance has now shrunk to 18.7%. Among other large movers, Amazon fell 3.9%, Meta dropped 5.9%, the AI cloud companies CoreWeave and Nebius fell 12.1% and 16.1%, and Intuit dropped 12.8% after cutting its annual revenue-growth forecast. Cryptocurrency-linked firms including Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood tumbled between 6.3% and 9.6% after bitcoin dropped below $60,000. The CBOE Volatility Index, Wall Street's fear gauge, soared 33% to 37, while the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note fell 12 basis points to 4.93% as investors sought safety.

"Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate earnings history; they did everything right. A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn't."

— Chuck Carlson, CEO, Horizon Investment Services

Sentiment, not earnings, is doing the damage

Strategists who spoke to Reuters largely said the AI trade's fundamentals had not broken, even as prices fell. "In the short run, sentiment drives prices. In the long run, fundamentals do. Right now the market is selling first and asking questions later," said Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager and partner at Founder ETFs. Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera, framed the week as two tests: "This week's chip earnings were an earnings test, and they passed it. Yesterday's AI IPO is a valuation test, and with the 10-year around 5% and the Fed still hiking, investors are asking how much of the AI story is already priced in." Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, described "an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," and said investors are broadly reducing exposure to technology and AI-related equities in favor of sectors such as health care, energy and utilities.

Rates are the other half of the story

The selloff is unfolding against a Federal Reserve that is still raising rates. Markets are pricing a near-certain likelihood of a 25-basis-point hike at the Fed's December meeting, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, and Fed Governor Lisa Cook said the central bank's policy rate was not sufficiently high to address elevated inflation. Next week's personal consumption expenditures figures will provide further clarity after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report. Breadth on Friday underlined the retreat: declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.77-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange, and volume on US exchanges was 25.19 billion shares, compared with the 19.50 billion average for a full session over the last 20 trading days.

What to watch next

Two questions now decide whether this stays a correction or becomes something deeper: whether the December hike lands as priced, and whether next week's PCE data gives the Fed reason to keep going in January. Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder, told Reuters the Fed is likely to raise rates at the December meeting and possibly in January as well. For long-term investors, several strategists argued the underlying earnings picture remains intact — chip earnings this week passed their test, in Goldman's words — but the valuation test the market is now running on AI stocks has further to go, and the indexes' record highs of last month will not be retested until it is done.
